items.title: Cursor ships two-way voice chat with coding agents, powered by a separate Grok Voice model that delegates to your coding agent
items.summary: In the Agents Window, IDE, web, and iOS, you can now hold a live voice call with your agent instead of typing. A dedicated Grok Voice model does the listening and speaking in real time; it hands off actual coding work to whichever model you've picked as your coding agent in that thread, then keeps talking with you while that agent works, checking a diff, confirming a run, or searching history via read-only lookups it can make directly. The coding agent decides what to say out loud; if it has nothing to say, the call reads back its usual written reply. Privacy Mode gives zero data retention.
items.why: A lightweight voice model that only talks and delegates, instead of trying to code itself, means the actual coding model never has to also be fast enough for live conversation -- a real pattern for anyone building a supervisor-plus-worker agent setup.
items.action: Next time you're away from the keyboard with a small, well-scoped change in mind, start a voice chat on a task and see how the hand-off between the voice agent and the coding agent actually feels in practice.

items.title: Google ships voice mode in Antigravity, built on Gemini Live -- one model does both the listening and the agent work, with voice locked out of anything destructive
items.summary: Antigravity's voice mode runs entirely on Gemini Live, which takes raw streamed audio directly rather than a text transcript. The same model keeps doing the actual agent work while talking, and you can interrupt it mid-sentence. Voice can approve ordinary actions but never anything destructive -- deleting files, elevated commands, a force-push -- those still require an on-screen click. Over SSH, the Antigravity CLI forwards your local mic and speaker to the remote agent.
items.why: It's a clean architectural contrast with Cursor's two-model design -- one model doing double duty, with permission scope enforced architecturally rather than by a second model's judgment.
items.action: If you use Antigravity, turn on voice mode for a routine fix-the-failing-test task and pay attention to exactly which step it still forces you back to the keyboard for.

eval.reason: Genuine new capability (Gemini Live raw-audio voice mode with permission gating), shipped Nov 5, not fluff.

items.title: Orca: a 119k-star multi-agent coding orchestrator that runs Claude Code, Codex, and other CLI agents in parallel, each in its own git worktree
items.summary: Hand Orca one big task and it splits the work, starts worker agents in their own isolated worktrees, and brings the results back to you -- chat or raw CLI, on your laptop, over SSH, or in the cloud with diffs and a browser in one app. A mobile app pings you when an agent needs input. Launched roughly three weeks ago and already at 119k stars, 7.5k forks, and nearly 20,000 commits of active development.
items.why: This is the same git-worktree-per-agent idea as the smaller worktrunk tool, but built out into a complete, massively-adopted product -- the apparent category leader for running several coding agents side by side.
items.action: Install Orca and hand it a task that naturally splits into independent pieces across your repos -- see how its worker-agent split compares to running the same task yourself in separate terminal tabs.

eval.reason: Real, massively-adopted multi-agent coding orchestration tool (119k stars, ~20k commits, active development); not a rehash of CodeGraph or Hindsight -- different category (fleet orchestration via worktrees).

items.title: Anthropic's engineering team explains "dreaming" -- how Claude reorganizes its own memory offline, and how it scaled a 350,000-file wiki from 13% to 48% accuracy over 128 sessions
items.summary: Surfaced via @AnthropicAI. Claude writes memory notes during a session, then uses idle time between sessions to "dream" -- rereading its own transcripts to catch and correct mistakes in those notes. In one test, Claude built and incrementally corrected a cross-referenced wiki over Anthropic's own 350,000-file internal document corpus; across 128 rounds of dreaming, accuracy on a 25-question eval set climbed from 13% to 48%. A separate test showed dreaming catching and fixing a wrong fact Claude had written mid-task, changing the outcome of a long-horizon task.
items.why: This is a real, tested architecture for giving an agent memory that improves itself over time instead of just accumulating -- directly adjacent to semantic knowledge-graph memory for cross-service code generation.
items.action: Read the wiki-building section closely -- the dreaming review/correction loop over a huge document corpus is a concrete pattern to test against your own code-knowledge-graph updates.

eval.reason: Substantive engineering writeup (memory consolidation, wiki-building at scale); not a duplicate of anything sent, distinct from the Nov 7 METR item.

items.title: Don't Vibe Code Your Agent Infrastructure -- Akshat Bubna, Modal
items.summary: Modal's CTO walks through what agent infrastructure actually needs once you're running many agents at once: a workspace per agent, state that persists for days without paying for idle compute, elastic GPUs, shared file systems for agents that collaborate, network controls, and observability agents can read themselves -- and makes the case against hand-rolling your own sandbox platform.
items.why: If you're building or extending an agent harness yourself, this is a checklist of the infrastructure decisions you'll eventually hit, from someone who's built this at scale.

items.title: How to Get Frontier Coding Results at 70% Lower Cost -- Nouha Dziri, Cohere
items.summary: A Cohere research scientist's findings from hundreds of experiments on ProgramBench and Commit0: multi-agent coding teams beat a single agent on long tasks but can cost several times more -- she maps where the extra workers pay off, including pairing a strong lead with cheaper planning workers to get close to an all-frontier team's results at roughly 70% lower cost.
items.why: A quantified, practical answer to whether it's worth running a team of agents instead of one -- exactly the tradeoff in designing a multi-agent coding harness.
